=== CALL C0097 ===
Jago: Hey! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Tereza: Yes, hi, I can hear you. Sorry, my camera was frozen for a second.
Jago: No worries, mine does that constantly. I'm Jago, by the way.
Tereza: Tereza. Nice to meet you.
Jago: Tereza, lovely. Did you do that puzzle bit at the start? I was proper rubbish at it, I just kept dragging things around hoping.
Tereza: Oh, the puzzle, yes. I think I did okay? I was very slow though, I like to check everything twice, so, erm... yeah. [laughs]
Jago: See, that's the sensible way. So where are you calling from?
Tereza: East London, Leyton. I'm originally from Czech Republic, from Brno, but I'm here eight years now.
Jago: Oh nice. I'm the opposite end of the country, Truro in Cornwall. Born and bred, never escaped. What do you do up there?
Tereza: I'm a clinical trials coordinator, at a hospital. So I schedule patients for their visits, I keep all the paperwork ready for audits, I process blood samples for the courier. It sounds boring, I know, but I quite like it. Somebody has to notice the missing signature, you know?
Jago: No, that's not boring, that's important. Honestly, I need someone like you in my life. I'm doing a film degree, final year, and I'm making a documentary about gig rowing, the old Cornish rowing boats, and the logistics side of it is just, like, chaos. Call sheets everywhere, tide times, I keep forgetting release forms.
Tereza: Release forms! That is exactly my job, consent forms. You must get them signed before, not after.
Jago: Yeah, I've learned that the hard way. [laughs] But the filming bit's proper good. I'm out on the water at six in the morning with these clubs, some of the rowers are in their seventies and they just tell you everything once the camera's on.
Tereza: That sounds lovely, actually. Six in the morning on the sea, though. Is it cold?
Jago: Freezing. I got soaked twice last week. Worth it though. I've sent it off to a couple of festivals, so fingers crossed, do you know what I mean?
Tereza: Oh wow, good luck. I would be too nervous to send something like that.
Jago: Oh, I'm bricking it, to be fair. Do you get back to Brno much?
Tereza: Twice a year, yes. I fly, but I'm terrible flyer, I hold the armrest like this the whole take-off. My husband laughs at me.
Jago: Ha. Have you done much travelling round Europe then? I interrailed for five weeks when I was twenty. Lisbon was my favourite, hands down.
Tereza: We went to Porto, me and Tom, for a long weekend. It was beautiful. The bridge, and the custard tarts, I ate maybe ten.
Jago: Only ten? Rookie numbers. No, Porto's meant to be unreal. I keep saying I'll go back to Portugal, and then Japan after I graduate, it's basically booked.
Tereza: Basically booked, or booked?
Jago: [laughs] Okay, it's in my head. That's basically booked.
Tereza: For me that is not booked. I plan everything months before, I have a spreadsheet for holidays. Is that strange?
Jago: No, that's amazing. Honestly, can I hire you? I'll pay you in pasties.
Tereza: Erm, I've never had real Cornish pasty, actually. Only the one from the train station.
Jago: Oh no. No, no, that doesn't count. You need to come down, I'll show you the proper place in Truro, there's a little bakery, it's—

=== CALL C0098 ===
Julie: Hello? Oh, hello, can you see me alright? Sorry, I wasn't sure which button.
Claire: Yes, you're fine, I can see you. I'm Claire.
Julie: Julie. Hello, Claire. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous with these video things, my son normally sets it up for me.
Claire: Don't worry, I nearly joined with my camera pointing at the ceiling. Where are you?
Julie: Basingstoke. I'm in the kitchen, you can probably see the fridge behind me, it's a bit of a state.
Claire: Ha, it's nowhere near as bad as mine. I'm in Faversham, in Kent.
Julie: Oh, lovely. Is that by the sea?
Claire: Sort of. It's on a creek, and there are marshes, and then the sea's a bit further out. I walk the dog out there most mornings. He rolls in anything dead, so it's not as idyllic as it sounds.
Julie: Oh, I saw the dog lead in your picture! I've got one too, Pip, Jack Russell cross. He's going grey round the muzzle now, bless him.
Claire: Mine's a terrier as well, Moss. Elderly and appallingly behaved. Is yours well behaved?
Julie: Erm, mostly. He barks at the postman. What do you do, Claire, if you don't mind me asking?
Claire: I've got an interior design studio in Canterbury with a business partner. I do the clients and the ideas, she does everything sensible. What about you?
Julie: I'm a care assistant, senior care assistant, at a care home. Older people, a lot of them with dementia. I've been doing it, oh, since my early forties. I came to it late, really.
Claire: How did you come to it?
Julie: Erm, well, I looked after my mum. She had dementia, and after she went I sort of thought, well, I know how to do this now, do you know what I mean? And I didn't want to go back to shop work. So I did my NVQs and that was that. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for a first chat.
Claire: No, not at all, that's a much better answer than most people give. It must be hard, though. Do you get attached?
Julie: Oh, terribly. You're not supposed to, but you do. There was one lady who used to call me "my Julie". When she passed I sat in the car park and cried my eyes out. The managers always say you get used to it, but you don't really.
Claire: No, I don't think you should get used to it, honestly. I'd worry about the ones who did.
Julie: That's what I think! Some of the agency staff, they just... anyway. Sorry, I've gone off on one.
Claire: You haven't. Are you working today?
Julie: I was on an early, so I'm absolutely shattered. I'll be asleep in front of Strictly by eight.
Claire: I don't watch it, I'm afraid. My daughter does, she's eleven, she does all the scoring with a little notepad.
Julie: Oh, bless her. That's what my granddaughter does! Has she got a favourite?
Claire: Probably. I'd be lying if I said I knew who it was.
Julie: [laughs] Well, you'll have to ask her and tell me. Is that... sorry, is that a painting behind you? It's very big.
Claire: It is. It's one of mine, actually. Half-finished, and crooked, as you can see. I keep meaning to—

=== CALL C0099 ===
Tomasz: Hello. Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah. Alright. I'm Craig.
Tomasz: Tomasz. Nice to meet you, Craig.
Craig: Yeah, you too.
Tomasz: So, er, where are you based?
Craig: Swindon.
Tomasz: Ah, Swindon. I'm in West London, Hanwell, near Ealing. Not too far, M4, yeah?
Craig: Yeah, straight down the M4. Hour and a half if it's quiet. It's never quiet though.
Tomasz: [laughs] No. To be honest, I drive to Heathrow most days for work, I know the traffic very well.
Craig: What is it you do?
Tomasz: I'm operations manager for facilities management company. So cleaning, maintenance, security, for office buildings. I have six site supervisors under me. Lots of phone calls, lots of emails, you know?
Craig: Fair enough. Sounds busy.
Tomasz: Very busy. And you?
Craig: Quality inspection. At an engineering firm. I run the CMM, the measuring machine, on machined parts, aluminium mostly. Check they're in tolerance, write up the reports.
Tomasz: Ah, okay, so very precise work.
Craig: Yeah, sort of. Had to redo a whole batch this week, to be fair, 'cause someone set the fixture up wrong. Every part out by the same amount.
Tomasz: That's painful. Who gets the blame for that?
Craig: Not me. Whoever set it up. I just measure it.
Tomasz: [laughs] Good answer. In my job, everything is my fault, you know? Toilet on fourth floor is broken, client calls me.
Craig: Yeah.
Tomasz: Er... you have a model car, I can see behind you. Audi?
Craig: Yeah, that's the quattro, the rally one. I've got an A3 myself. Ten years old, but I keep it proper clean. Just put new tyres on it, weren't cheap.
Tomasz: Tyres are crazy now. I have company car allowance, so I'm driving Skoda Superb at the moment, but I'm looking at the new models online every evening. My wife says I should marry the car.
Craig: [laughs] Yeah, I'm the same with BMW listings. Looking at a 3 Series, maybe. Saving for a house first, though.
Tomasz: Sensible. House first. We bought in 2019, it's hard, the deposit. You are renting?
Craig: Er, living with my parents at the moment. Just while I save. It's sensible, yeah.
Tomasz: Of course, very sensible. In Poland this is completely normal, nobody judges.
Craig: Yeah. Fair enough.
Tomasz: Do you do the gym? You look like you train.
Craig: Three times a week. Mostly weights. Headphones in.
Tomasz: Same, three mornings, before work. And the rowing machine. We just got new ones, very nice, with screens.
Craig: Ours has been rammed since January. Can't get on anything.
Tomasz: January people. By March they're gone, yeah?
Craig: Hopefully, yeah.
Tomasz: Er, so the puzzle at the beginning, did you finish it?
Craig: Most of it. Didn't really read the instructions, to be honest.
Tomasz: [laughs] I read them three times and still I was not sure if I did it right. Is it—

=== CALL C0100 ===
Jago: Hiya! Oh, hello. Can you hear me?
Julie: Hello, love, yes, I can hear you. Sorry, I've just got my glasses on, hang on. There we go. I'm Julie.
Jago: Jago. Nice to meet you, Julie.
Julie: Jago, that's an unusual one, isn't it? Is that Cornish? Sorry, I saw the surf bits in your photo.
Jago: Yeah, spot on, it's Cornish. I'm in Truro. My nan picked it, basically. Where are you?
Julie: Basingstoke. Nothing exciting. Roundabouts, mostly.
Jago: [laughs] I've driven through it, I think. Loads of roundabouts, yeah. How's your day been?
Julie: Erm, alright. I was on an early, so I've been up since half five. I'm a care assistant at a care home. I'm absolutely shattered, to be honest, so if I start yawning it's not you.
Jago: No, fair play, that's proper hard work. My mum works at a GP surgery, she's the office manager, so she's always telling me what the care homes ring up about. Do you like it?
Julie: I do, yeah. I love the residents. It's the staffing that gets you, you know, when you're short and you've got twelve people to get up and dressed and their breakfasts, and the agency girl's on her phone. But the residents themselves, bless them, they're lovely. Some of them have got the best stories. One gentleman was in the war, and he still flirts with all of us.
Jago: See, that's what I love. I'm doing a film degree, and my final project's a documentary about gig rowing clubs, and the best bits are always the older lot. There's this fella, he's seventy-four, and he just sat in the boat shed and told me about rowing to the Scillies back in the eighties. I didn't have to ask him anything, I just pointed the camera.
Julie: Oh, that's lovely. That's what's missing, isn't it, people just listening to them.
Jago: Exactly that. You could probably make a better film than me, to be honest, you've got all the stories.
Julie: Oh, no, I wouldn't know where to start. I can barely get this laptop working. My son set it up.
Jago: How old's your son?
Julie: Liam's twenty-eight. He still lives with me, him and his girlfriend. He leaves his work boots right in the hallway, every single day. I've nearly gone flying three times this week.
Jago: [laughs] Oh, that's me. My mum would say exactly the same. I'm twenty-three and still at home, still having her roast every Sunday. I'm never moving out at this rate.
Julie: Well, why would you? A roast every Sunday, I'd stay. Does she do Yorkshires?
Jago: Massive ones. And she does the roast potatoes in goose fat, they're unreal.
Julie: Oh, she sounds like she knows what she's doing. I do mine in the oil, I can't stretch to goose fat with the price of a shop now.
Jago: To be fair, I think she only does it at Christmas, I'm embellishing. [laughs]
Julie: [laughs] I knew it! You've got that look. You remind me a bit of my Liam, actually, the hair. Sorry, is that a weird thing to say?
Jago: No, that's a compliment, I'll take it. Funnily enough, I said you looked like my mum on that photo bit.
Julie: Oh, bless you. Well, I hope she's—

=== CALL C0101 ===
Tomasz: Hello, good evening. Can you hear me?
Tereza: Yes, hello. I'm Tereza.
Tomasz: Tomasz. Nice to meet you.
Tereza: Nice to meet you. Erm, Tomasz, is that Polish?
Tomasz: Yes, Polish, from Rzeszów. And you? I can hear a little accent also.
Tereza: Czech, from Brno. So we are almost neighbours. [laughs]
Tomasz: Ah, very good. Neighbours in London as well, maybe. Where are you?
Tereza: Leyton, East London. And you?
Tomasz: Hanwell, West. Other end of Central line.
Tereza: Oh, the Central line. In summer it's like a sauna, I come to work completely melted.
Tomasz: Yes! This morning it was rammed, I was standing with somebody's elbow in my face. Usually I drive, I have company car, but today it was in for valeting.
Tereza: Okay. What is your job, sorry?
Tomasz: Operations manager, facilities management. Office buildings, cleaning, security, maintenance. I have six supervisors. And you?
Tereza: I'm clinical trials coordinator at a hospital. Paperwork, patient visits, samples. Very organised, very boring for other people. I just told the last person, he did film, and he has no release forms. [laughs]
Tomasz: [laughs] Ah, the young guy with the surfboard?
Tereza: Yes. He's very nice, but I think he needs a spreadsheet.
Tomasz: For me, spreadsheets are life, to be honest. Budgets, contracts, everything. When contract renewal is coming, I'm checking my phone at midnight. My wife is angry with me.
Tereza: Me too, before audits I can't sleep. I make a checklist, and then a checklist for the checklist. How long are you in London?
Tomasz: Eighteen years. I came at nineteen. First job, I was cleaning offices at night. Then porter, then supervisor, and now, you know, manager. Step by step.
Tereza: Wow. That's a really big journey. I came eight years ago, just for one year. And now I am married to an Englishman, so... [laughs]
Tomasz: Ah, so you stay. My wife is Polish, we speak Polish at home, but our daughter, she's five, she answers me in English now. Every time. It's strange feeling, you know?
Tereza: I can imagine. We don't have children yet, but I think about this, which language, where to live, near my mum or here. Sorry, that's a lot.
Tomasz: No, no, it's normal. I think about this also. Sometimes I feel not properly Polish, not properly British. Somewhere in the middle.
Tereza: Yes, exactly that. When I go home, my brother says I talk like a tourist.
Tomasz: [laughs] My sister says the same. Do you go back for Christmas?
Tereza: Yes, every year. Carp, potato salad, cookies. My mum starts baking in November.
Tomasz: Same, but with us it's the twelve dishes, and barszcz with uszka. And Midnight Mass, my mum makes us go. Is that okay, what I said? You are religious, maybe not?
Tereza: Not really, no, but I like the traditions, the food especially. I saw your—

=== CALL C0102 ===
Claire: Hello. Can you hear me?
Craig: Yeah. Alright. Craig.
Claire: Claire. Hi.
Craig: Hi.
Claire: So, where are you?
Craig: Swindon.
Claire: Okay. I'm in Faversham, Kent. Have you been?
Craig: No. Don't think so.
Claire: No, most people haven't. It's nice. Small. Lots of pubs. Erm, what do you do, Craig?
Craig: Quality inspection. Engineering firm. Measuring parts, basically.
Claire: Measuring parts. Measuring them for what, though? Sorry, I genuinely don't know what that involves.
Craig: Er, so we machine aluminium parts, for other companies, and I put them on the CMM, it's a coordinate measuring machine, it probes the part and tells you if every dimension's in tolerance. Like, if the drawing says a hole's ten mil, plus or minus a couple of microns, it checks it is. Then I write it up.
Claire: Microns. God. That's quite satisfying, actually, isn't it? Either it's right or it isn't.
Craig: Yeah, sort of. Mostly. Sometimes it's borderline and the manager wants it out the door anyway.
Claire: And do you let it go?
Craig: Er, yeah, usually. If it's that close. Not my call, to be fair.
Claire: Hm. I'd be awful at that. I'm in interior design, and I'd never be allowed near anything measured in microns. I eyeball everything. My business partner measures things twice and then measures my measurements.
Craig: Fair enough.
Claire: Do you enjoy it?
Craig: It's alright. Pays okay. I'd want the next grade up, though. Quality engineer. Better money.
Claire: That's a very honest answer. Most people would say they're passionate about it.
Craig: Not really passionate. It's a job, yeah.
Claire: No, I respect that. What do you do when you're not measuring?
Craig: Gym. Bit of gaming. Cars, mostly. Got an A3, I keep it clean.
Claire: I don't know anything about cars. Mine's a Volvo full of dog hair and crisp packets. My son would probably love you, he's fifteen, all he talks about is cars and football.
Craig: Who does he support?
Claire: Arsenal, I think. Or he did. He has it on constantly and I find it unbearably boring, I'm sorry.
Craig: [laughs] That's alright. I support Swindon. Most people find that boring.
Claire: Are they any good?
Craig: No. Lost again Saturday.
Claire: [laughs] Well, at least you're loyal. Why do you keep going?
Craig: Er, I go with my dad. Few times a season. It's more that, really. He's got bad knees now, so...
Claire: That's nice, actually. That's a proper reason. I'll stop being snooty about football, then. Sort of. Did you do that puzzle at the start, by the—

=== CALL C0103 ===
Jago: Hey, how's it going? Can you hear me alright?
Tomasz: Yes, hello. I can hear you. Tomasz.
Jago: Jago. Nice to meet you, mate.
Tomasz: Nice to meet you. Er, I think I already heard about you, actually. The documentary, with the boats? And the release forms?
Jago: [laughs] Oh no. Tereza's been talking, has she? Yeah, that's me. In my defence, I've got them all signed now. Most of them.
Tomasz: Most of them. [laughs] Okay. In my job, "most of them" is a problem, you know?
Jago: Yeah, fair. What is it you do?
Tomasz: Operations manager. Facilities management, for office buildings in west London and Heathrow. Cleaning, security, maintenance contracts. I have six site supervisors. Company car, lots of emails, phone never stops.
Jago: Proper grown-up job, then. That's the bit I'm dreading, to be honest, the actual career part. I'm in my last year, and all my mates from school are in London already, in offices, and I'm still here doing bar shifts on a Saturday.
Tomasz: How old are you?
Jago: Twenty-three.
Tomasz: Twenty-three is nothing. At twenty-three I was cleaning offices at night. I came here at nineteen with, er, one bag. Then porter, then supervisor, step by step. So you are not behind, I think.
Jago: Oh, that's mad. From cleaning to running the whole thing? That's a proper story, that. I'm not even joking, that's the kind of thing I'd want to film.
Tomasz: [laughs] Nobody wants to watch film about toilets on fourth floor.
Jago: You'd be surprised, mate. People love behind-the-scenes stuff. Actually, does your company do any video? Like, recruitment videos, or showing clients what you do? Because that's exactly the sort of branded content I want to get into after I graduate, documentary-style, real people, not cheesy stock footage.
Tomasz: Er, we have one video on website, it's very old. Some man in a suit walking in a corridor. To be honest it's terrible.
Jago: See, I could sort that. Just saying. I've got a Sony FX3, gimbal, drone licence, the lot.
Tomasz: Okay, maybe. I can mention to the directors. I'm not promising, yeah? It's a budget question.
Jago: No, course, no pressure. Do you get much time off, with all that?
Tomasz: Gym three mornings, before work. Saturday I take my daughter swimming. And once a year we go all-inclusive, Crete or Turkey. Last year I booked the premium room, sea view, private pool. Very nice.
Jago: Private pool, look at you. I've only ever done hostel bunks. Interrailing, five weeks, Lisbon, Berlin. Slept on a floor in Prague one night.
Tomasz: No, no, no. I did the floors when I was young. Now I want the good hotel. [laughs]
Jago: That's earned, though, isn't it, honestly. Do you follow any football? I play five-a-side on a Wednesday.
Tomasz: Brentford, a little bit, because it's local. Sometimes a supplier gives us tickets for a box.
Jago: A box! Mate, you're living the dream. I watch the rugby in the pub with a—

=== CALL C0104 ===
Julie: Hello? Oh, hello, can you hear me? Sorry, I keep leaning into the screen.
Craig: Yeah. Alright. I'm Craig.
Julie: Julie. Hello, Craig. Have you had a good day?
Craig: Yeah, not bad. Bit long. Work, then this.
Julie: Oh, same. I was on an early. What is it you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Craig: Quality inspection. Engineering. Measuring parts.
Julie: Measuring parts. Oh, right. For cars, or...?
Craig: Er, all sorts. Aluminium bits, for other firms. Some go into car stuff, yeah.
Julie: My son would like that. He's a forklift driver, at one of the warehouses, but he's mad on cars. He's always on about some engine or other and I just nod. Sorry, I don't know anything about it.
Craig: That's alright. What's he drive?
Julie: Erm, it's a Golf, I think? A black one. He's always washing it on the drive and leaving the bucket out.
Craig: Golf's a good car. Sensible. I've got an A3, same sort of thing underneath.
Julie: Oh, is it? There you go, I've learned something. Where are you, Craig?
Craig: Swindon.
Julie: Oh, Swindon, I've been through there, there's that magic roundabout, isn't there? I went round it twice and came out the wrong way.
Craig: [laughs] Yeah, everyone does. The roadworks on the A419 are worse, to be fair. Doing my head in.
Julie: Oh, I can imagine. We've got the same in Basingstoke, they dig a road up, fill it in, then dig it up again a week later. Do you live on your own, or...?
Craig: Er, with my mum and dad at the moment. Saving for a deposit.
Julie: Oh, well, that's very sensible. My Liam's still with me at twenty-eight, him and his girlfriend. I don't mind, really, it's nice having the house full. Does your mum still cook for you?
Craig: Yeah. Most nights. She keeps putting extra veg on my plate.
Julie: [laughs] Good for her! I do exactly the same. I hide it in the shepherd's pie, carrots and that, he doesn't even notice.
Craig: Yeah, mine does that with the chilli. I've noticed.
Julie: [laughs] Oh dear. Well, she means well.
Craig: Yeah. I've been helping out more, to be fair. My dad's knees are going, so I do the bins, the garden, that sort of thing.
Julie: Oh, that's good of you. That's really good. I work with older people, I'm in a care home, and the ones whose families do the little things, it makes all the difference, you know. Has he seen anyone about the knees?
Craig: Er, he's on a list. Physio, I think.
Julie: Make sure he keeps moving, even just a little walk. That's what they always tell our lot. Sorry, I'm going into work mode.
Craig: No, that's alright. That's useful, yeah.
Julie: Have you got any holidays planned? Something to look forward to?
Craig: Thinking Tenerife again. September. Been three times, same place.
Julie: Oh, I don't blame you, if you know it. I'm terrible with flying, I check the passports about ten times before we even leave the—

=== CALL C0105 ===
Tereza: Hello! Can you hear me?
Claire: Yes. Hi, I'm Claire.
Tereza: Tereza. Nice to meet you. Sorry, I'm a bit close to the camera.
Claire: You're fine. Where are you?
Tereza: Leyton, East London. And you?
Claire: Faversham, in Kent. Little market town. You have a lot of books behind you.
Tereza: Oh, yes. [laughs] Too many. Mostly crime, Scandinavian crime. And some Czech ones, I'm from Brno. I'm in a book club at the library.
Claire: What are you reading at the moment?
Tereza: For book club it's literary one, about a family in Ireland, it's very slow. Honestly I'm finding it a little bit boring, but I can't say that at book club, everybody loves it.
Claire: Why can't you say that?
Tereza: Erm... I don't know. I don't want to be the difficult one, I think.
Claire: You should say it. Book clubs are much better when somebody hates the book. Otherwise it's just everyone nodding over biscuits, you know.
Tereza: [laughs] Maybe. I bring the cake, so maybe they forgive me.
Claire: Exactly. That's your leverage. What do you do, for work?
Tereza: Clinical trials coordinator, at a hospital. Very organised job, lots of checklists. I plan everything. Even holidays, I have a spreadsheet.
Claire: God. I'm the opposite. I book things the night before. I once nearly missed a ferry to France because I hadn't checked the kids' passports, and my son's had expired. We were in the queue at Dover, and I was sort of arguing with a man in a booth, and in the end we had to drive to the passport office in Peterborough the next morning. The holiday started two days late.
Tereza: Oh no. That is my absolute nightmare. I would be crying in the car.
Claire: The kids loved it, actually. They thought it was an adventure. My daughter didn't, she's very tidy, she was furious with me. Rightly.
Tereza: [laughs] Maybe she should do your spreadsheets.
Claire: She probably will, eventually. Where do you like to go?
Tereza: We went to Porto, me and my husband. And Lake District, walking. And I go home to Brno twice a year.
Claire: Porto's lovely. I prefer Lisbon, though, honestly. It's scruffier. Porto's a bit too pleased with itself.
Tereza: Oh. Erm, I liked it. But I haven't been to Lisbon, so I can't say.
Claire: Go, and then tell me I'm wrong. People always say I'm wrong.
Tereza: [laughs] Okay, I will put it in the spreadsheet. Sorry, can I ask, the painting behind you, is it yours?
Claire: Yes. It's not finished. I've got about six in the spare room in the same state.
Tereza: It's beautiful, the colours. Why don't you finish them?
Claire: [pause] I don't really know. I think if I finish them I have to decide if they're any good. Which is a bit—

=== CALL C0106 ===
Jago: Alright, mate! Can you hear me okay?
Craig: Yeah. Alright. I'm Craig.
Jago: Jago. Last call of the lot, I think, isn't it? How you finding it?
Craig: Yeah, alright. Bit weird, talking to strangers for three minutes.
Jago: It is a bit, yeah. Like speed dating but nobody's allowed to fancy anyone. I'm down in Truro, Cornwall. Where are you?
Craig: Swindon.
Jago: Swindon, nice. Have you ever been down Cornwall?
Craig: Newquay. Stag do. Don't remember a lot of it, to be fair.
Jago: Ha, classic. I did a whole summer season at a surf hostel in Newquay, and honestly the stag dos were the best and worst bit of the job. Every Friday, a minibus of lads in matching T-shirts, someone dressed as a banana, and by Sunday someone's lost a shoe on Fistral beach. No offence, like.
Craig: None taken. We were probably one of them.
Jago: [laughs] Was there a banana?
Craig: Mankini, I think.
Jago: Even worse. What do you do then, Craig?
Craig: Quality inspection. Engineering firm. I run a CMM, measuring machine, checking parts are in tolerance.
Jago: Oh, so properly precise. I'm the opposite, I just point a camera and hope. Is that a gaming headset behind you? Are you a gamer?
Craig: Bit, yeah. Racing sims mostly. Some shooters. Mic off.
